newsitem.title: UK: Mark exodus ahead of EMU overstated, say analysts.
newsitem.headline: Mark exodus ahead of EMU overstated, say analysts.

text.p: Concerns over a flight out of German marks ahead of European economic and monetary union (EMU) appear to be overstated at the moment, currency analysts said on Thursday.

Such flows out of Germany into EMU safe-haven currencies like sterling, Swiss francs and the dollar have already taken place, albeit gradually, but are more the result of redirecting new money rather than a wholesale reversal out of German assets, they said.

The anti-mark theme reappeared after a prominent EMU critic, Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen, said on Wednesday there were signs that investors were transferring funds out of the mark ahead of EMU althought there was no sign of a major shift.
"This is not fresh news, it is known that central banks and institutions have been lightening up their mark exposure," said Nick Parsons, foreign exchange strategist at Paribas in London.
"People have been going into Swiss francs, sterling and the dollar but this has been more a commitment of fresh funds into new markets rather than active disinvestment (out of Germany)."
Still, whenever a member of the German central bank talks about the mark, currency dealers listen.

"The fact that a Bundesbank member has acknowledged the possibility of a capital flight out of the mark is clearly grist to the mill of those who believe the onset of EMU is beginning to undermine investor confidence," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.

While this could result in a higher risk premium on German assets, Meggyesi said that if nervousness over EMU was great enough to shift investors out of marks, "Bundesbank compliance in a run on the mark cannot be taken for granted."

Renewed optimism for a timely start to EMU with a broad-based membership is currently running high, which has boosted the asset markets of borderline first-wave EMU members like Italy, Spain and Portugal.
This has come at the expense of the mark as such a broad-based membership is seen diluting the strength of the euro.

"If it is perceived EMU is going ahead, then the best place to park your money is in a safe haven," said Stewart Newnham, economist at First Chicago. "The incentives for (foreign) investment into EMU Europe are negative at the moment."

This, so far, has not resulted in a run on the mark and EMU optimism has kept the German unit in fairly close proximity to the Exchange Rate Mechanism central rates for most of the EMS bloc -- the expected basis for conversion to the euro in January 1999.

This shadowing of central rates is expected to continue with any untoward exchange rate movements expected to be ironed out by the central banks, all keen to ensure the transition to the euro is smooth.
While this is good for the single currency project, there are few investment opportunities left as Europe's financial markets grind closer to convergence, analysts said.
The risk of an EMU delay, which would probably see knee-jerk flow into marks, still haunts the market and, analysts say, will continue to provide a steady base for German currency.
